newsitem.title: POLAND: Jewish property body says reached deal with Poland.
newsitem.headline: Jewish property body says reached deal with Poland.

text.p: The World Jewish Restitution Organisation (WJRO) said on Wednesday it had reached an initial agreement with Poland on the return of communal property and if this proved successful the body would not argue against Polish entry to NATO.

"If we are invited to give testimony (to U.S. Congress and Senate committees), and if this (Polish) government understanding with us holds as now, we will certainly give a positive report," WJRO Vice-President Naphtali Lavie told Reuters by telephone in Warsaw.

The Warsaw parliament this year passed a law on relations with the nine small remaining Jewish congregations in Poland, paving the way for the return of some of the communal property that belonged to Jewish organisations before World War Two.
Most of Poland's 3.5 million Jews were murdered by wartime Nazi German invaders, others later emigrated, and properties were taken over by the then communist authorities.

The Israel-based WJRO, an international umbrella group for Jewish bodies, was dissatisfied with the Polish proposals partly because it estimates there are more former synagogues, schools and other such properties than the government says.

Lavie was reported in Polish news media last month as saying the WJRO, linked with the U.S.-based World Jewish Congress (WJC) may oppose ratification by the U.S. Senate of Poland's entry to the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
NATO leaders at their Madrid summit on Tuesday invited Warsaw, Prague and Budapest to start entry talks but all 16 parliaments must give their approval.
As the crucial vote in the U.S. Senate next year needs two-thirds support to pass and could be close, the WJRO stance caused consternation in Warsaw.
Lavie said his earlier remarks had been quoted out of context and had applied largely to a dispute with Romania now being settled.

"If this agreement holds water, there is no reason why we should make any negative comments," he said of the deal with Poland which has yet to be finally approved by an organisation grouping Jewish religious communities in Poland now numbering about 3,000 mostly elderly people.

Under the agreement reached late on Tuesday the WJRO, Polish Jewish communities and the Polish government will set up a foundation to agree on and handle properties being returned, along lines adopted in Hungary and being discussed in Romania.
A joint commission will study a list of 6,000 properties identified by the WJRO and decide which claims can be processed, Lavie said, adding this would take a long time.

He said that while his talks with Interior Minister Leszek Miller and other officials this week had not settled all points the Polish side had shown good will. Polish government officials were not immediately available to comment.
Apart from the communal properties, the WJRO also wants Poland to in some way restore to the community heirless private properties once belonging to Jews who died in the Holocaust.
But Lavie said the WJRO would address this issue only when Poland passed a general law on reprivatisation of private property taken by the communists, which is proving difficult.
